title: DVFS & Power Guidance for A100 / H100 / L4 / MI300 — Serving Runtime
content:
Purpose:
This note captures practical guidance and experimental observations for using DVFS (clock scaling) and power capping on common GPUs in our fleet (NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, NVIDIA L4, AMD MI300) with the Redwood serving runtime. The goal is to provide safe defaults and operational heuristics for Dedicated and Private deployments to improve cost-efficiency while avoiding tail-latency regressions and thermal issues.

Scope and constraints:
- Applies to inference workloads typical for token generation and chat (variable sequence lengths, KV cache use).
- Focus on steady-state throughput latency tradeoffs; short transient behavior (first token, cold start of model) also called out where relevant.
- We assume up-to-date drivers/ROCm and kernel modules; specific commands are included.
- Hardware differences are emphasized; do not assume a one-size-fits-all clock/power profile.

Executive summary (recommended defaults):
- A100 (40/80GB): Default to fixed power cap at 300W for long-running model servers where density matters. If latency SLO is tight (<50ms at 1-token), allow up to 350W but watch thermal throttling. Use persistent max GPU clock only for high-concurrency batchers.
- H100: Prefer dynamic clocking with aggressive thermal headroom. Baseline cap at 350–400W depending on PCIe vs SXM; for SXM allow 450W for critical latency-critical customers. H100 benefits more from higher SM clocks for transformer kernels; small token latency improves measurably.
- L4: Keep default vendor profiles (auto boost) and cap power at 150–175W. L4 is designed for power-efficient inference; avoid forcing max clocks as occupancy is usually lower.
- MI300: Use ROCm-clocks and set power profiles at 320–360W for sustained throughput. MI300 shows best perf when memory clocks are stable; avoid frequent DVFS transitions.

Why these choices: practical tradeoffs
- Power caps reduce tail-power draw and datacenter cooling costs but can lower peak SM/mem clocks and increase latency for single-token and small-batch cases.
- H100’s transformer kernels are highly sensitive to SM clock; modest increases (5–10%) in SM clock often yield larger reductions in p50/p95 for single-token generation than equivalent increases in batch concurrency.
- L4’s memory-subsystem constraints mean memory-clock increases often show diminishing returns; focus on batching and kernel-fusion instead.

Commands and telemetry (quick reference):
- NVIDIA (nvidia-smi):
  - query clocks/power: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,index,clocks.sm,clocks.mem,power.draw,temperature.gpu --format=csv -l 1
  - set application clocks (A100/H100): sudo nvidia-smi -i <gpu> -ac <memClock,graphicsClock>
  - set power cap: sudo nvidia-smi -i <gpu> -pl <watts>
  - persistence mode: sudo nvidia-smi -i <gpu> -pm ENABLED
- AMD/MI300 (rocm-smi):
  - list clocks/power: /opt/rocm/bin/rocm-smi --showclocks --showpower
  - set clocks/power: /opt/rocm/bin/rocm-smi --setsclk <level> --setmclk <level> --setpoweroverdrive <val>

Perf counters & signals to monitor (enable in runtime telemetry):
- GPU: SM_usage (active cycles), memory_utilization, mem_bw_utilization, sm_clock, mem_clock, power_draw, temperature
- Kernel-level: tensor_core_util, occupancy %, warps_active, l2_hit_rate
- Runtime: request_queue_length, batching_latency_ms, kv_cache_hit_rate, p50/p95 single-token latency, p99 tail latency

Experimental methodology notes (how we measured):
- Use stable trace-replay of production traffic (same sequence length distribution and prompt fanout).
- Warm KV cache for minority of experiments to measure realistic fast-paths.
- Run each configuration for minimum 10 sustained minutes after warm-up; measure p50/p95/p99 and power draw.
- Collect GPU telemetry at 1s granularity.

Representative observations (high level numbers from internal runs):
- H100 SXM at 400W vs 350W: p50 single-token reduced by ~8–12% at same QPS; p99 improved by ~6%. Power draw increased ~10–12W on average.
- A100 300W vs 350W: throughput for small-batch (batch_size=4) improved ~7% at the higher cap; tail-latency reduction smaller (3–5%).
- L4: raising mem_clock showed <3% throughput gains for transformer models with large KV cache; better gains from increasing batch concurrency.
- MI300: stable mem_clock eliminates periodic stalls observed when the card switched power states under bursty traffic.

Scheduling and runtime behavior recommendations:
1) Avoid per-request clock changes. Changes to DVFS or power caps are slow (100s of ms to seconds) and will destabilize tail latency. Always apply DVFS changes at deployment or maintenance windows.
2) Use node labels and routing policies: tag nodes with hardware and chosen power profile (e.g., h100-lowlatency-450W, a100-density-300W) and route latency-critical routes to higher-power nodes.
3) Batchers should be clock-aware: if running on a high-power profile, favor smaller max_batch_size to reduce latency; on low-power density nodes, prefer larger max_batch_size to amortize memory bandwidth costs.
4) KV cache placement: co-locate long-lived KV cache with the serving process pinned to the GPU that has a stable clock profile; frequent context migration between GPUs with different clocks increases cold-KV misses and CPU/GPU synchronization overhead.

Kernel-level tuning knobs (practical):
- Prefer tensor-cores / FP16 where model and quality allow. On H100, TF32-to-FP16 fallback is common; ensure kernel selection favors tensor-core fused kernels for matmuls.
- For A100/H100, keep large-ish occupancy to exploit tensor cores — tune threads/block and smem usage in custom kernels.
- Avoid forcing absolute max SM clocks for low-utilization pods; the cosmetic latency improvement is small but increases site power.

Operational playbook (step-by-step suggestions):
1) Baseline run: collect full telemetry over a 30-min replay; record p50/p95/p99, power, temps.
2) Power-cap experiment: incrementally raise/lower -pl by 25W steps; run 10m stabilized windows; collect delta in p50/p95 and power cost.
3) Clock experiment (NVIDIA only): use -ac to set mem/graphics clocks; prefer setting persistence mode first.
4) Classification: if p95 improves >5% with <8% power delta, consider promoting profile to latency pool.
5) Rollout: phased update using routing policies and canary sampling (5%, 20%, 100%). Observe p99 before final rollout.

Edge cases and cautions:
- Thermal throttling on oversubscribed racks can create non-deterministic performance cliffs; rely on temperature and thermal margin telemetry to detect early.
- On multi-tenant nodes, per-GPU power capping still interacts with chassis-level power budgets; coordinate with infra.
- ROCm-tooling for MI300 sometimes reports clocks differently; prefer long-run averages and mem_bw signals to evaluate real impact.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Investigate automated RCAs: can we classify a request as "power-limited" vs "compute-limited" using runtime counters and route accordingly?
- Explore micro-DVFS: small clock nudges between request bursts (subject to stability checks) — useful for bursty traffic? Needs safety harness.
- Tune KV cache eviction heuristics for heterogeneous clock profiles to avoid prefetch churn.

Appendix: sample experiment commands and logging config
- Start telemetry: /opt/redwood/bin/telemetry-agent --gpu-metrics --interval=1s --out /tmp/gpu-metrics.log
- Run replay: /opt/redwood/bin/trace-replay --trace traces/prod-2025-11-01.json --concurrency 16 --duration 1800
- Apply power cap (example): sudo nvidia-smi -i 0 -pl 350
- Snapshot stats: cat /tmp/gpu-metrics.log | jq -s '.' > /tmp/gpu-agg.json

Concluding notes:
This document is a working reference — it is intentionally pragmatic and conservative. H100 delivers the largest per-watt single-token improvements when allowed higher clocks; L4 is optimized for density and benefits more from batching and kernel-level fusion than DVFS. MI300 requires careful ROCm tuning to avoid state thrash. Document next steps: run controlled experiments for two production models (chat-medium and embeddings-heavy) across the four GPUs and capture full-week telemetry under each profile.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Run MI300 long-tail stability run (48h) with static mem clocks and submit findings to CONFLUENCE-RT.
- Add per-model recommended profile table after two more model runs.
- Share playbook with SRE and Capacity teams and capture chassis-level power interactions.
